title: Design Number Container System
description:
# Design Number Container System

Design a number container system over positive integer indices.

Each index can store at most one number at a time. Calling `change` on an index that already stores a number replaces the old number with the new one. A later `find(number)` call must only consider the current number stored at each index; stale assignments from earlier changes must not be returned.

Implement the `NumberContainers` class:

*   `NumberContainers()` initializes the system.
*   `void change(int index, int number)` stores `number` at `index`, replacing the previous value at that index if one exists.
*   `int find(int number)` returns the smallest index currently storing `number`, or `-1` if no index currently stores `number`.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["NumberContainers", "find", "change", "change", "change", "change", "find", "change", "find"]
[[], [10], [2, 10], [1, 10], [3, 10], [5, 10], [10], [1, 20], [10]]
**Output**
[null, -1, null, null, null, null, 1, null, 2]
**Explanation**
`find(10)` first returns `-1` because no index currently stores `10`. After indices `2`, `1`, `3`, and `5` are set to `10`, the smallest such index is `1`. Then `change(1, 20)` replaces the value at index `1`, so index `1` no longer belongs to number `10`, and the next `find(10)` returns `2`.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= index, number <= 10^9`
*   At most `10^5` calls will be made to `change` and `find`.

solutions.name: TreeSet of Indices per Number
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per change, O(1) per find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain `indexToNumber`, plus a map from each number to a `TreeSet` of indices currently storing that number. On `change`, remove the index from the old number's set if it had one, then add it to the new number's set. `find` returns the first index in the target number's set.

## Key Insight

The reverse map must represent current ownership only. Removing the index from its old number before inserting into the new number prevents stale assignments from being reported later.

## Complexity Analysis

Each update performs at most one deletion and one insertion in ordered sets, so it costs O(log n). Reading the smallest index is O(1). The maps store one current index entry, so space is O(n).

solutions.name: Lazy Min-Heap per Number
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per change, amortized O(log n) per find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep the current number for each index in a map. For every number, keep a min-heap of indices that have ever been assigned to that number. `change` only updates the current map and pushes the index into the new number's heap. `find` removes heap tops whose current map value no longer matches the queried number.

## Key Insight

A priority queue cannot cheaply delete an arbitrary stale index from an old number. Lazy deletion leaves stale indices in place but proves they are harmless by checking the current `indexToNumber` map before returning.

## Complexity Analysis

Each update pushes one heap item in O(log n). Each stale heap entry is popped at most once, so queries are amortized O(log n). Old snapshots may remain, so space is O(n + q).

solutions.name: Global Ordered Number-Index Records
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per change and find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store every current assignment as a `Record(number, index)` inside one global `TreeSet` ordered first by number and then by index. Also keep `indexToNumber` so a replacement can remove the old record. To find a number, seek the first record at least `(number, 0)` and verify that the number matches.

## Key Insight

One global ordered set can answer all number queries if the sort order groups equal numbers together and sorts their indices increasingly inside the group.

## Complexity Analysis

Changing an index removes and inserts one record, both O(log n). `ceiling` for a query is O(log n). The structure stores one current record per assigned index, so space is O(n).

solutions.name: Indexed Min-Heap per Number
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per change, O(1) per find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Each number owns a custom min-heap of its current indices. The heap also stores a position map from index to heap slot, so `change` can remove an index from its old number's heap in O(log n) before adding it to the new number's heap. `find` reads the root of the heap.

## Key Insight

This is the non-lazy heap route: every heap contains only live indices. The position map is what makes arbitrary removal practical.

## Complexity Analysis

Removing from one heap and adding to another each costs O(log n). Querying the heap root is O(1). Each active index appears in exactly one heap, so space is O(n).

solutions.name: Dynamic Segment Tree per Number
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log U) per change, O(1) per find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat indices as a sparse coordinate range from `1` to `10^9`. Each number owns a dynamic segment tree whose root stores the minimum active index for that number. Changing an index removes it from the old number's tree and inserts it into the new number's tree. `find` reads the root minimum.

## Key Insight

The index domain is huge, but at most `10^5` operations appear. Dynamic segment trees allocate only nodes along updated paths, while still supporting direct maintenance of the minimum active index.

## Complexity Analysis

Each insertion or deletion touches O(log U) nodes, where `U = 10^9`. Querying the root is O(1). Space is proportional to the number of update paths that have been created.
